events.text: Dark, and warm, and a heartbeat bigger than the world. Something rough as a pine cone goes over you from tail to ears, again and again, until you squeak. Your mother's tongue. Around you three other small bodies push for the milk, and one of them has already found out that ears are for biting.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Push for the milk with the rest

effects.log: You are the smallest, so you push hardest. By the end of the first week you have a place at the milk of your own and a scratch on your nose to prove it.

choices.text: Find the quiet place under her chin

effects.log: Under her chin it is still, and her breathing goes over you like wind over a ridge. You will look for that kind of quiet all your life.

choices.text: Bite back

effects.log: You bite the ear that bit you. Its owner squalls, and your mother licks you both flat. Somebody had to be the first to learn that biting back is a choice. It was you.

events.text: On the tenth day the dark comes apart. A grey crack, then a smear of light where the den opens on the hill, then shapes: your mother, enormous, striped like the shadow of a bamboo grove; and three cubs, all bigger than you. The biggest has paws like rice paddles. One has a notch in its ear already. One just watches you, without blinking.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Look at the light first

effects.log: You stare at the den mouth until your eyes water. Out there is white and green and moving. It is the first thing you ever wanted.

choices.text: Look at your mother first

effects.log: She looks back with eyes the colour of autumn honey and licks your face, once, as if checking that the eyes work. They do.

choices.text: Look at the three of them, and learn which is which

effects.log: Broad-Paw, the biggest, who sits on everyone. Torn-Ear, who bites. Hush, who watches. Your three brothers. You will be learning which is which for the rest of your lives.

events.text: Your mother carries you to the mouth of the den by the scruff of your neck and sets you down on the edge of the world. It is white. It falls out of the sky in pieces, without a sound, and the pieces land on your nose and vanish. Behind you Broad-Paw is already sneezing.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Bite the snow

effects.log: It bites back, cold, and is gone. You bite it again. You bite snow all afternoon and catch none of it, and you are happier than you have ever been.

choices.text: Put one paw in it, carefully

effects.log: Your paw goes down and down and does not stop. You pull it out with great dignity and sit on it. Your mother makes a coughing sound you will later learn is a tiger laughing.

choices.text: Go back in. It is too big

effects.log: You back into the warm dark and watch the white from there. Some creatures run at the world. You will always look at it first. It is not cowardice. Your mother does exactly the same.

events.text: A morning of hard frost. The others wake and push for the milk. The smallest cub does not. It lies in the corner where the cold came in, and it is you: you can see the den from somewhere a little above it, quite calmly, the way the magpie on the oak must see it. Your mother noses the small body once, twice. Then she lies down around it and begins to lick.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Go back down into the small body

ok.log: It is like climbing into a wet sack. Then a heartbeat, then a second one, then her tongue, rough as a pine cone. You squall. She keeps licking until you are angry, which is how she knows you are alive. (-10 health)

fail.log: You fall back in sideways and hurt everywhere. It takes the whole day, and your mother does not stop licking once. By night you are warm. You are never quite as warm again. (-20 health)

choices.text: Follow the warmth: Hush has pressed against you

effects.log: Hush, who watches, has crawled over and lain on the small cold body without being told. The heat comes through his fur into yours, and you come back for it. Hush never mentions it, in the way tigers do not mention things. (-10 health)

choices.text: Look up first: something is writing

effects.log: Above the snow, above the oak, an old hand with a brush is about to strike a name off a long list. It stops. It writes a small note in the margin instead. Then you are in the den again, screaming, and your mother is licking you. (-12 health)

events.text: The smell of men comes up the hill on a south wind: smoke, sweat, iron, dog. Your mother is on her feet before it has finished arriving. She picks the cubs up by the scruff, one by one, and carries them over the ridge to a crack in the rocks above a stream. You are last.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Hang limp, the way a cub should

effects.log: You hang like a wet stocking and she carries you fast. Behind you the dogs find the old den and bark into it all afternoon. There is nobody in it.

choices.text: Wriggle round to see where you are going

effects.log: Upside down, you learn the ridge, the saddle, the stream, the crack in the rock. You will walk that way alone one day, and know it.

choices.text: Wonder why she took you last

effects.log: Because you were the smallest, and the smallest are the easiest to leave. She came back for you anyway. You think about that for years.

events.text: Your mother teaches without a sound. She goes down into the snow until her belly is in it and her shoulders are higher than her back, and moves forward one paw at a time, setting each hind paw down exactly where a forepaw was lifted. Ahead, at the edge of the birch wood, a roe deer scrapes for moss. Behind her, you try.

choices.text: Copy her exactly, paw for paw

ok.log: Paw, paw, breath, paw. The snow does not creak. The deer does not lift its head. Your mother looks back at you once, and the look is the first praise you remember.

fail.log: Your hind paw lands on a twig the snow has hidden. Snap. The deer is a white rump bobbing away through the birches. Your mother sighs through her nose, which is worse than a cuff.

choices.text: Go faster: the deer will leave

effects.log: You go faster. The deer leaves faster. You are learning that the hunt is mostly the part before the hunt.

choices.text: Watch her, not the deer

effects.log: She never looks straight at it. She looks at the place where it will be. You fall asleep that night practising looking at nothing.

events.text: A boar trail through the oaks, and the wind is wrong: from behind you, carrying your smell ahead of you like a gong. Your mother stops. She turns round and walks you all the way back down the ridge and round the far side of the hill, a whole morning's walk, so that the wind comes into your face.

choices.text: Complain the whole way round

effects.log: You grumble round the entire hill. At the end of it the boar is still there, rooting, with no idea. Your mother takes it in one rush. You stop complaining.

choices.text: Lift your nose and read the wind

effects.log: The wind in your face is full of news: boar, rotten acorns, a fox, last year's rain. The wind at your back only tells everyone about you.

choices.text: Try the short way alone

ok.log: The wind drops just as you get there. You stand nose to nose with a young boar, equally astonished. It runs. You run. You both tell it differently afterwards.

fail.log: The boar smells you at forty paces, waits, and comes at you through the ferns. Your mother arrives before the tusk does, nearly. (-8 health)

events.text: A doe and her fawn at the salt lick in the gully. Your mother is flat in the bracken beside you. She looks at you, then at them, and does not move. Today the hunt is yours: yours to start, and yours to aim.

choices.text: The doe: more meat, and the fawn will not live alone

effects.log: The rush, the doe, your mother finishing it. The fawn stands in the gully until dusk, bleating, and then it is not there. You eat well. You remember the bleating longer than the meal.

choices.text: The fawn: it is easier, and the doe can have another

effects.log: The fawn is quick and over quickly. The doe stands on the ridge above and looks down at you. She will have another. She looks as if she knows it, and that it does not help.

choices.text: Neither. Let them go

effects.log: You lie still until they leave. Your mother looks at you for a long time. That night there is nothing to eat, and she does not hunt for you. A tiger who spares must also be a tiger who goes hungry.

events.text: In the warm part of an afternoon your mother lies on her side on a flat rock, and you find the scar under the fur of her shoulder: a pale, puckered seam as long as your paw. A spear, once, from a man in a brushwood blind. It smells of nothing now. But it is in the way she still will not cross the valley road by daylight.

choices.text: Lick the scar

effects.log: She lets you. It does not need licking. Some things you do because they need doing, and some because the one you love has a scar.

choices.text: Learn the lesson in it: stay off the road

effects.log: She never crosses the valley road in daylight. Neither, from now on, do you. Somewhere in a county office a count of tigers is one shorter for it.

choices.text: Learn a different lesson: men can be killed

effects.log: She did not kill the man with the spear. You decide, without being told, that you would have. It is the first hard thing you ever decided.

events.text: It happens on an ordinary morning. You come back to the rock with a hare, and your mother is waiting on it, and she does not move aside. Her ears go flat. When you take one more step her teeth close on your shoulder: not hard, then hard. Behind her, in the den, something small is crying. A new litter.

choices.text: Go. Do not look back

effects.log: You go down the far side of the ridge with the hare still in your mouth and do not look back once, and you are very proud of that until about noon.

choices.text: Look back once, from the ridge

effects.log: She is still on the rock, watching you. She does not call. A tigress who drives her cubs away is not done loving them. She is done raising them.

choices.text: Stand and fight her for the rock

effects.log: She is twice your weight and it is over in three breaths. She leaves you bleeding in the bracken and goes back to the crying. That is the last lesson and the hardest: she was right. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave the hare on the rock for the new ones

effects.log: You put it down at her feet and back away. She looks at the hare, then at you, for a long moment. Then she picks it up and goes into the den. You walk down the mountain hungry, and somehow fed.

events.text: Years later, on the far side of the mountain, you cross a scent on a boundary oak that you know before you know why: pine, blood, warm dark. Her. Old now, and slow, marking a smaller territory than she used to. She is drinking at the stream below you, and the spear scar on her shoulder has gone white.

choices.text: Go down and lie beside her

ok.log: She lifts her head, smells you, and does not flatten her ears. You lie on the stones beside her and drink, two tigers, not talking. When you leave she licks your face once, rough as a pine cone. It is the last time.

fail.log: She does not know you. Her ears go flat and she snarls, the snarl of an old tigress tired of the young. You go. That was the whole point of driving you off: that one day she would not know you. (-6 health)

choices.text: Drive the deer down to her side of the stream

effects.log: All that winter the deer somehow cross to her side of the mountain. She eats. She never knows. That is how she did it for you.

choices.text: Leave her be

effects.log: You watch until she goes back into the trees. Some debts are never paid to the one you owe. You will pay this one to cubs that are not born yet.

events.text: Broad-Paw sits on you. That is his whole method: he is the biggest, he sits, and you are under him until he gets bored. Torn-Ear bites ears, tails, paws, whatever is nearest, and does not stop when you squeal. Hush does not play. Hush watches who wins.

choices.text: Bite Broad-Paw's tail until he gets off

effects.log: He gets off. He also gets back on, harder, later. You learn that winning once is only an invitation.

choices.text: Get out from under by going limp

effects.log: He waits for the struggle, which does not come, and loses interest. Boredom, you discover, is a weapon.

choices.text: Go and sit beside Hush and watch

effects.log: Hush moves over a little to make room. Together you watch Broad-Paw sit on Torn-Ear, which is much more fun from outside.

events.text: Torn-Ear comes back from the lower ridge at dawn with something in his mouth: a straw sandal, frayed, black with charcoal dust. It smells of smoke and sweat, and of something else, warm and salty, that you have never smelled before. He drops it in front of the three of you like a prize. "From the charcoal man on the next ridge," he says. "Taste."

choices.text: Taste it

effects.log: Salt, and smoke, and a sweetness under it that your mouth remembers long after you want it to. Torn-Ear watches your face and grins. Hush does not taste. Hush watches you.

choices.text: Push it away

effects.log: You push it back across the stones with your nose. Broad-Paw takes it instead and chews it to pieces. Torn-Ear looks at you as if you had said something rude.

choices.text: Bury it

effects.log: You dig a hole under the roots, drop the sandal in and cover it. Torn-Ear does not stop you. He laughs. "Bury it all you like," he says. "The charcoal man is still on the next ridge."

choices.text: Ask what happened to the charcoal man

effects.log: "Nothing," says Torn-Ear. "Yet. He ran. He ran right out of his sandal." He finds that very funny. Broad-Paw finds it funny because Torn-Ear does. Hush says nothing.

events.text: The three of them go down to the edge of the village at dusk now, to the place where the children come out for firewood. They lie in the millet and watch. They do not do anything, yet. Every evening Torn-Ear looks back up the hill at you and waits to see whether you will come.

choices.text: Go with them, to watch

effects.log: You lie in the millet with your brothers and watch a girl with a bundle of sticks walk home singing. Your brothers watch her the way they watch deer. You watch her the way you watch the snow: something you do not understand, that you are not sure you should touch.

choices.text: Stay up the hill

effects.log: Torn-Ear stops looking back after the third evening. Hush keeps looking back a little longer.

choices.text: Go down and break it up: roar in the millet

ok.log: You roar from the edge of the field, a young roar, cracked in the middle. The children drop their sticks and run. Your brothers turn on you, and Broad-Paw sits on you for a long time. The village bars its gates for a month. Nobody is eaten.

fail.log: Your roar comes out a squeak. The children laugh. Your brothers do not; they drag you back up the hill by the scruff and leave you bleeding on the rocks. (-10 health)

events.text: Your brothers are grown, huge, and they have gone down the mountain for good. The talk in the forest is of three tigers far in the south, in the hills above a great city with a stone pagoda, who take people off the roads at night: three brothers, always together, and the villages there have stopped counting. You were not with them. You are the one who did not.

choices.text: Be glad of it

effects.log: You are glad. You are also, at night, a little lonely, which is the price of being the one who did not.

choices.text: Go south to see them, once

effects.log: Nine days south, and you find them in a bamboo grove above a city of tiled roofs and a pagoda as tall as a pine. They are fat and glossy and they smell of the city. Torn-Ear offers to share. You go home the next morning, the long way, through the hills.

choices.text: Wish that heaven would stop them

effects.log: You say it aloud to the night, in the way of tigers. Somewhere far above, a brush pauses over a page, as if someone had heard. It is not stopped yet. It will be. You do not know yet what that will cost.

events.text: One winter Hush comes back up the mountain alone, thinner, with a cut across his nose and the smell of the city on him. He lies down outside your den in the snow, the way he once lay on you when you were cold, and does not explain.

choices.text: Let him in

effects.log: He sleeps for three days. On the fourth he says, "Torn-Ear eats too many. Someone will come for us." Then he goes south again, because they are his brothers too. You keep the warm side of the den for him for years.

choices.text: Ask him to stay with you

ok.log: He stays a whole season. You hunt together, which you never did as cubs, and he is very good at it, quietly. In spring he goes south. "They will not last without someone watching," he says. He is right, and it will not be enough.

fail.log: "I cannot," he says. "Someone has to watch them." He goes in the night without waking you, which is the kindest way he knows.

choices.text: Send him back. You chose

effects.log: You stand in the den mouth until he goes. He goes without a word, the way he does everything. You tell yourself it was just. It felt only cold.

events.text: A winter night, and you have come down further than you are allowed: right into the village, into the yard of a thatched house, under a paper window full of lamplight. Strings of shrivelled orange things hang from the eaves. Inside, a baby is screaming. "Hush, the tiger is coming!" says its mother. The baby screams louder, not even slightly afraid of you. "Hush, here is a gotgam," says the mother, and the screaming stops dead, as if cut with a sickle. Whatever a gotgam is, it is worse than a tiger.

choices.text: Run. Now

effects.log: You go over the wall in one leap, the best leap of your life so far. Behind you the village sleeps, with a gotgam in it somewhere.

choices.text: Hide in the dark by the cowshed and think

effects.log: You slip round to the cowshed, between a dozing ox and the wall, and think very hard about what kind of creature silences a baby that a tiger cannot.

choices.text: Stay and see the gotgam

ok.log: You wait all night. The gotgam does not show itself. That is the most frightening thing of all. You creep away before dawn, having seen nothing, and later tell your brothers it was enormous.

fail.log: A dog comes round the house, sees you, and howls like a person. Lamps everywhere. You run, and somewhere behind you, you are sure, the gotgam is getting up.

events.text: A few nights later you are back, because you cannot help it, lying low in the dark by the cowshed, still thinking about the gotgam, when a hand comes over the wall. A man, feeling his way in the black with a rope over his shoulder: a cow thief, looking for the biggest beast in the yard. His hand finds your back. It is broad and furry and warm. "Good," he whispers. "A fat one." And he swings himself up onto you.

choices.text: The gotgam! Run!

effects.log: You go out of that yard like a stone from a sling, with the gotgam clinging to your fur. Over walls, through the stubble, up the mountain. It does not let go. It is the longest night of your life.

choices.text: Roll on it

ok.log: You drop and roll. The gotgam makes a very human noise and loses its grip, and for one breath you are free. Then it is back on you, hands in your fur, and you run anyway. You are not stupid.

fail.log: You roll and it holds on, wailing. It has hands like iron. You give up and run, with the gotgam riding. (-6 health)

choices.text: Freeze and wait for it to eat you

effects.log: You freeze. The gotgam kicks you in the ribs to make you go. You go. Neither of you is enjoying this.

events.text: Grey light. The thing on your back has gone very quiet. Then, as you pass under an old zelkova at the foot of the hills, the weight is suddenly gone: it has grabbed a branch and hauled itself up into the hollow of the trunk. You run on, lighter, thinking: it fell off. I am saved. Behind you, in the tree, a cow thief who has just seen what he rode all night sits in the hollow and shakes.

choices.text: Keep running and never look back

effects.log: You run until noon and sleep in a ditch. For the rest of your life you will not go near a house with orange things hanging from the eaves.

choices.text: Turn round and look at the tree

effects.log: In the hollow is a man, a perfectly ordinary man, grey with fright, holding a rope. Not a gotgam. You look at each other for a long moment. He tries to climb further in. You sit at the bottom and work it out, slowly, and are not sure which of you was the bigger fool.

choices.text: Wait under the tree for the gotgam to come down

effects.log: It does not come down. You wait all day. At dusk the villagers come with gongs and you leave, still not knowing what it was. In the village a cow thief swears he will never steal again, and keeps his word.

events.text: A magpie lands on the pine above your den and laughs: the dry rattle magpies have, like stones in a gourd. It laughs at you, and then it flies to the next pine and tells someone, and laughs again. By evening every bird on the mountain knows about the tiger that ran from a dried persimmon with a cow thief on its back.

choices.text: Pretend it never happened

effects.log: You walk about the mountain with great dignity for a month. The birds go quiet as you pass and start again behind you.

choices.text: Climb the pine after it

ok.log: You get halfway up before the branch bends. The magpie hops one branch higher, considers you, and laughs louder.

fail.log: You fall out of the pine into a snowdrift. The magpie has to sit down. (-5 health)

choices.text: Laugh too

effects.log: You lie on your back in the snow and make the coughing sound your mother made at the den mouth. The magpie stops, puzzled. A tiger that laughs at itself is no fun at all. It flies away to find someone prouder.

events.text: There is a magpie on the pine above the den. As far as you can tell it has been there since the day you were born. It comes down when you pounce on a frog and miss, sits on a root a tail's length away, tilts its head at you, and makes a noise like stones rattling in a gourd. It is laughing.

choices.text: Pounce on the magpie

ok.log: You come down with one long black tail-feather in your mouth. The magpie, from the pine, is furious. You sleep with the feather under your paw for a month.

fail.log: You land where the magpie was. It is now on your head. You did not feel it land. It laughs from there.

choices.text: Ignore it

effects.log: You go back to the frog. The magpie follows you all morning, commenting. You catch the frog at last, and the magpie stops laughing, and you are surprised at how much you wanted it to.

choices.text: Bring it something

effects.log: You leave the back half of a frog on the root. The magpie looks at it with contempt and eats it. The next morning it is back on the pine, and it does not laugh. Well. It laughs less.

events.text: The magpie comes down the slope in a flurry, shrieking, and does not stop: down to your den, up to the pine, down again. Below in the valley, faint, you hear it too: a gong struck in time, dogs, and men calling to each other in the long voices of beaters. A hunt, coming up the gully.

choices.text: Trust the magpie: over the ridge, now

effects.log: You are over the ridge before the dogs reach the den. They find only the old smell of you, and the magpie on the pine scolding them, which they hate.

choices.text: Go and look first

ok.log: From a rock above the gully you count them: twelve men, four dogs, spears and two bows and a drum. Then you go. You will remember how a hunt sounds when it is coming.

fail.log: A dog sees you on the rock. You go back up the hill with the pack behind you and an arrow singing past your ear. The magpie screams the whole way, as if to say: I told you. (-10 health)

choices.text: Lie flat in the den and hope

effects.log: The dogs come to the den mouth and bark into it. Your heart beats so loud you are sure they hear it. The men decide the den is old and go on up the gully. The magpie says nothing at all, pointedly.

events.text: You follow the magpie one evening, just to see where a magpie goes. It goes up: past the tree line, past the rocks, to an old pine on the shoulder of the mountain where a heap of stones stands with a strip of white cloth tied to it. Under the pine sits an old man with a white beard and a staff, very still. The magpie lands on his shoulder. You blink, and there is nobody under the pine but snow.

choices.text: Go up to the stones

effects.log: There is nobody. There is a smell of pine resin and old paper and something like your mother. On the top stone the magpie sits alone, looking at you as if you had arrived exactly on time.

choices.text: Put your chin on your paws, the way cubs greet their mother

effects.log: You lay your chin on your paws in the snow. Nobody is there to see it. Somebody sees it anyway.

choices.text: Back away down the hill

effects.log: You do not know what you saw, so you leave it there. The magpie does not laugh at you on the way home. That is how you know it was something.

events.text: You have killed a big boar, alone, and you are lying on the carcass in full view on the ridge, letting the whole mountain see. The magpie lands on the boar's snout, an arm's length from your face, looks at you, then at the boar, then at you, and laughs until it nearly falls off.

choices.text: Snap at it

effects.log: It is gone before your teeth close and back on the boar's tail before they open. You learn nothing, which the magpie seems to find even funnier.

choices.text: Get off the carcass and drag it into the trees

effects.log: A tiger lying on its kill in the open is a story for every hunter in the valley. You drag it into the trees. The magpie follows and eats some. That seems to be its fee.

choices.text: Leave it a share

effects.log: You tear off a strip of fat and leave it on a rock. The magpie eats it, wipes its beak on the stone, and flies off up the mountain toward the old pine, as if to report.

events.text: The magpie on the pine has news. It always has news. Today it is shouting it at you from three branches up, hopping, and pointing its beak down the valley.

choices.text: Go and see

ok.log: A red deer with a broken leg in the gully, and nobody else has found it yet. The magpie takes its share first.

fail.log: A woodcutter asleep under a tree with his lunch beside him. You look at the magpie. The magpie looks at the lunch. You leave the two of them to it.

choices.text: Ignore it. Magpies lie

effects.log: Magpies do not lie. They exaggerate. You find out that evening that there really were hunters on the south slope, but only two, and lost.

choices.text: Shout back

effects.log: A young tiger and a magpie shouting at each other across a pine wood for half a morning. The deer for a mile around leave. Nothing is learned. You both feel better.

events.text: Deep winter, and you are hungry, and you have caught a rabbit at last: a fat brown one with one bent ear, round as a rice ball, under your paws. "Wait," says the rabbit, very fast. "Wait, wait, wait. A tiger your size, eating one small rabbit? I know where there are fish. Hundreds of fish. A tiger could eat fish all winter. Let me show you."

choices.text: Eat the rabbit

effects.log: One small rabbit. It is gone in three bites and you are still hungry. You will never know about the fish. Some part of you will always wonder.

choices.text: Let it show you

effects.log: You let it go. It does not run, which surprises you. It hops ahead down to the frozen stream, looking back to make sure you are following, like a host.

choices.text: Keep one paw on it, and let it talk

effects.log: You keep a paw on its back. It talks all the way down to the stream: fish, fish, the fattest fish in the province. You are a little bewitched. That is the idea.

events.text: At the frozen stream the rabbit shows you a hole in the ice the size of a bowl, black water moving under it. "Put your tail in," it says. "Fish bite tails. Everybody knows that. Sit very still all night, and do not move whatever you feel, and in the morning, pull. Your tail will be heavy with fish." The night is very cold. The rabbit sits on the bank to watch.

choices.text: Put your tail in and sit all night

effects.log: You sit. The water is cold, then colder, then nothing at all. Things tug at your tail: fish, surely. Your tail grows heavy, heavier. You do not move. You are going to eat so well.

choices.text: Make the rabbit put its tail in first

effects.log: The rabbit looks at its tail, which is the size of a pinch of cotton, and then at you. "Mine is too short," it says with great dignity, and hops off into the dark. You go to bed hungry, and whole.

choices.text: Put the tip in, and keep watching the rabbit

ok.log: Toward midnight the edges of the hole start to whiten and close. You pull your tail out just in time and look at the rabbit, and the rabbit looks at you, and leaves at great speed.

fail.log: You watch the rabbit so hard you forget the ice. When you look down, the hole has closed round your tail like a fist.

events.text: Dawn. You pull, and your tail does not come. It is in the ice to the root, frozen solid. The rabbit is gone. And on the far bank, coming down to the stream with a water jar on her head, is a village woman, who stops.

choices.text: Pull with everything you have

effects.log: You tear free and leave half the fur of your tail in the ice, a striped ring of it, frozen there for the village children to find. The woman drops her jar. You run up the mountain bald-tailed and furious. The fur grows back by summer, a shade paler at the tip. (-12 health)

choices.text: Lie still and wait for the sun

ok.log: The woman backs away up the path without a sound and does not come back. By noon the sun has softened the ice and you slide free with all your fur, and a lesson.

fail.log: She runs for the village. Men come with poles. You tear loose before they arrive and leave half your tail-fur behind. A boy keeps it in his house for years, as proof. (-10 health)

choices.text: Roar until the ice cracks

effects.log: You roar at the ice. It does not care. The woman cares very much, and is gone. In the end you thrash free and leave a ring of striped fur behind. Somewhere a rabbit is telling this story. (-6 health)

events.text: Your mother comes back from the gully with a young hare in her mouth, alive, and puts it down in front of the cubs. It sits there, stunned. Then it bolts. Broad-Paw falls over Torn-Ear. Torn-Ear bites Broad-Paw. Hush simply watches where it goes. And you:

choices.text: Chase it straight

ok.log: You get a paw on it in the bracken and it gets out from under. You get a paw on it again. In the end your mother finishes it for you, but the paw was yours.

fail.log: It goes left. You go straight. It is a long way to the bottom of the hill, and you go all of it.

choices.text: Cut across to where it is going

effects.log: You go where Hush is looking. The hare comes round a rock straight into your chest. You are both very surprised, and you let go out of surprise. Still: you were there.

choices.text: Watch your mother, not the hare

effects.log: She is not watching the hare either. She is watching the four of you, one at a time, and you see her decide something about each of you. You do not know what she decided about you.

events.text: Frost on the grass at the edge of the birches. A young roe deer, alone, head down, a stone's throw off, and the wind in your face. Your mother is somewhere behind you and has not moved. This one is yours or nobody's. Your legs have started to shake.

choices.text: Wait until your legs stop shaking

ok.log: They do not stop. You go anyway, at the very moment the deer lifts its head, and it is under you before it knows. Your first kill. Afterwards your mother comes out of the trees and licks your face and says nothing, and it is enough.

fail.log: You wait too long. The deer looks straight at you and is gone in three bounds. You lie in the frost until your mother comes and nudges you up. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go now, before your nerve goes

ok.log: You go in an untidy rush, half pounce and half fall, and somehow the deer is under you, and then it is still. Your first kill. You stand over it shaking from nose to tail. Your mother licks your face.

fail.log: The deer kicks out as you land and you take a hoof in the chest. It is gone. You are on your back, staring at the sky. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it go: not today

effects.log: You stand up and let it see you. It goes. Your mother comes out of the trees and looks at you a long time. There is no shame in it. There is no meat in it either.

events.text: A young boar alone in the oak mast, digging, its back to you. It is small, for a boar. You have watched your mother take three of them. You go, and it turns, and it is not small at all from the front.

choices.text: Go for the neck, as she does

ok.log: Teeth in the thick of the neck, paws round the shoulders, and you hold on through the worst ride of your life until it stops. You lie beside it for an hour, not eating, just breathing.

fail.log: The tusk opens your flank from shoulder to hip. You get away up a slope it cannot climb fast and lie there bleeding until your mother finds you. You have a scar now, like her. (-20 health)

choices.text: Leap clear and let it go

effects.log: You jump sideways as it charges, and the tusk goes past your belly by a hair. It does not chase you. Boars do not need to. (-5 health)

choices.text: Run it into the thornbrake

ok.log: You lead it in a circle into a thicket where it cannot turn, and then you are on its back. Clever, your mother's look says later. Not brave. Clever is better.

fail.log: The thorns are worse for you than for the boar. It goes through them like a cart. You come out scratched to the eyes. (-12 health)

events.text: You have made your first kill, and now you have to eat it: the first meat in your life that nobody caught for you. Your brothers have smelled it and are coming through the bracken. The magpie is already on a branch. Your mother is lying a little way off, not helping, watching to see what you will do.

choices.text: Eat first. It is yours

effects.log: You eat until you cannot, growling at everything that moves. Your brothers wait. When you are done they fall on what is left. Your mother says nothing. That is also an answer.

choices.text: Share with your brothers

effects.log: You step back. Broad-Paw takes the best part, of course. But Hush, for the first time, eats beside you, and Torn-Ear is too surprised to bite anyone.

choices.text: Carry the first bite to your mother

effects.log: You put the first piece down in front of her. She looks at it, and at you, and pushes it back with her nose. Then she eats a little anyway, so as not to shame you. The first meat you ever caught, and you gave the first of it away.

choices.text: Leave a share on the rock for the magpie

effects.log: A strip of meat on the flat rock. The magpie takes it and flies, not to its own nest, but straight up the mountain toward the old pine, as if delivering it.

events.text: Autumn, the game trail along the gully, and a patch of leaves that looks exactly like every other patch of leaves. It is not. The ground drops out from under you and you fall twice your own height into a pit dug by men, with earthen walls too straight to climb and the sky a square of blue far above.

choices.text: Leap for the rim, again and again

effects.log: You get your claws over the edge once and hang there, and fall back. Again. Again. By dark your claws are torn and you are still in the pit. (-8 health)

choices.text: Dig at the walls

effects.log: The earth is packed hard and only crumbles near the top, where you cannot reach. You dig a hollow the size of yourself and lie in it. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lie still and save your strength

effects.log: You lie at the bottom and watch the square of sky go from blue to gold to black. Someone will come, men or something else. You will need your strength either way.

events.text: Two days. On the third morning a face looks over the rim: a thin traveller with a wooden A-frame on his back, a salt peddler by the smell of him. He stares down at you. You stare up. You cannot speak to him, and he knows it, but he talks anyway, as people do to animals: "Poor thing. If I let you out, you will eat me. Will you eat me?"

choices.text: Look up at him as pitifully as a tiger can

effects.log: You put your head on your paws and look up. It works far better than it should. He sighs, says "I am a fool," and goes to find a log.

choices.text: Roll over and show your belly

effects.log: A tiger showing its belly. He laughs, a little wildly, says "All right, all right," and drags a fallen pine log to the rim.

choices.text: Roar at him

effects.log: He jumps back from the rim. A long time later he comes back with a log anyway. "You are frightened," he says. "So am I. Come on."

events.text: You come up the log and over the rim onto solid ground, and the hunger of three days comes up with you. The peddler sees it in your face and backs against a pine. "No," he says. "That is not fair. Let us ask someone." And the pine answers, though only you can hear it: eat him; men cut us for their houses and their fires and their coffins, and never once say thank you. An old ox grazing in the stubble below lifts its head and says the same: I ploughed for them twenty years, and now they are fattening me for the pot. Eat him.

choices.text: They are right. Eat him

effects.log: You crouch. The peddler shuts his eyes. Then something small and brown hops out of the bracken between you, sits up on its haunches, and asks a question.

choices.text: Two judges are not enough. Wait for a third

effects.log: You sit down, which surprises the peddler and you. A tree and an ox have spoken. A case should have three. As if it had been waiting for exactly that, a rabbit hops out of the bracken.

choices.text: The pine and the ox are bitter. Do not listen

effects.log: A tree that hates the axe and an ox that hates the pot are not judges; they are plaintiffs. You turn away from the peddler. Before he can thank you, a rabbit hops out of the bracken, sits up, and asks a question anyway.

events.text: It is a rabbit, brown, with one ear bent. It may be a rabbit you know. Rabbits all look alike to a tiger, and they like it that way. "I do not understand," it says, in a small slow voice. "Who was in the pit? You? How deep is the pit? Show me exactly how it was. I cannot judge what I have not seen."

choices.text: Show it: jump back into the pit

effects.log: You leap down into the pit to show exactly how it was. "Ah," says the rabbit from the rim. "So that is how it was." The peddler pulls the log up. "Then let it stay how it was," says the rabbit, and the two of them are gone.

choices.text: See the trick, and let it work anyway

effects.log: You see exactly what the rabbit is doing. You jump into the pit anyway. The log comes up. The rabbit looks down at you a moment longer than it needs to, and you think it knows that you knew. Then it goes.

choices.text: See the trick, and refuse

effects.log: You do not jump. You look at the rabbit, the rabbit looks at you, and then it is gone into the bracken like a thrown stone, and the peddler is gone the other way down the hill, faster than a man with a pack should be able to run. Nobody is eaten. Nobody is grateful.

events.text: It rains for two days and the pit walls slump, and on the third night you scramble out over the mud, filthy and starving. The peddler's tracks go down to the valley road, the road goes to a village, and in the village there is a house with a salt sack drying on the fence. You can smell him from the ridge. It is your first real verdict, and nobody will ever know how you gave it.

choices.text: Hunt him. He left you in the pit

effects.log: You go down at dusk and wait by the fence. When he comes out into the yard, you show yourself, all of you, at the end of his own garden. You do not touch him. You do not need to. He leaves the village within the month, and the story he tells about you is not the one he told about the rabbit.

choices.text: Let it go. He let you out

effects.log: He let you out. A rabbit put you back. The account is even, and you are the only one who knows it. You turn up the mountain, hungry, and for once it feels like the right kind of hungry.

choices.text: Leave a roe deer by his fence, for the log

effects.log: You kill a roe deer in the hills and leave it under the salt sack. In the morning the whole village comes to look at it, and at the tracks. The peddler sits on his doorstep for a long time. That winter he tells the story of the pit with the true ending, and nobody believes it.

choices.text: Hunt the rabbit instead

ok.log: You find it in the clover at dawn. It sees you and does not run. "Fair," it says. You eat it. It was. You are not at all sure that you won.

fail.log: You never find it. Rabbits are hard to find when they have a reason. You think of it every time the clover moves.

events.text: You ate a boar too fast, and a bone has gone in crosswise at the back of your throat: a long splinter of leg bone, wedged. You cannot swallow, and you cannot close your mouth. By the second day you cannot drink, and you find yourself walking down the mountain without knowing why, toward a smell of lamp oil. The light is a hermitage: a hut against the cliff, a stone lamp, a pile of books, and {npc}, a poor student studying for the state examination up here alone, because the hermitage costs nothing. {He} looks up from the book and sees a tiger in the yard with its mouth open and its eyes full of water. {He} does not run. {He} puts the book down very carefully and rolls up a sleeve.

choices.text: Hold your mouth open and trust {him}

mem.note: pulled the bone out of its throat

effects.log: A hand goes into your mouth, finds the bone, works it, pulls. It comes out with a sound like a cork, and the pain goes with it. {npc} sits down in the yard, shaking, holding the bone up to the lamp, and starts to laugh. (-6 health)

choices.text: Shut your eyes. You cannot watch

mem.note: pulled the bone out of its throat

effects.log: You feel the hand, the pull, the sudden emptiness where the pain was. When you open your eyes {npc} is washing {his} hands in the stream, talking to the stream quite calmly about the classics, as if nothing had happened. (-6 health)

choices.text: Growl a warning first

mem.note: pulled the bone out of its throat, growling

effects.log: You growl so {he} knows what {he} is doing. {He} knows. "Yes, yes," {npc} says. "I know. Hold still." The hand goes in. The bone comes out. {npc} wipes {his} hands on the robe with great care, and only then sits down very suddenly. (-6 health)

events.text: You owe {npc} a life, and tigers do not know how to say so. {He} is still at the hermitage, still studying, eating millet gruel and wild greens and getting thinner over the books. In the mornings {he} leaves the gate open, and sometimes {he} talks to the trees in case you are listening.

choices.text: Leave a pheasant at the gate every few days

mem.note: left game at my gate all winter

effects.log: Pheasants, a hare, once a whole roe deer that {npc} cannot lift. {He} eats better than any student in the province, and studies harder, and tells nobody where the meat comes from.

choices.text: Lie by the wall at night while {he} reads aloud

effects.log: You lie in the dark outside the wall and listen to {npc} read the classics aloud half the night, every night. You do not understand a word. You learn the shape of the sentences the way you learned the shape of the wind.

choices.text: Keep the wolves off the hermitage

effects.log: The wolves of that side of the mountain learn very quickly where not to go. {npc} wonders why the nights are so quiet, sleeps better, and dreams of a tiger.

events.text: Spring of an examination year. {npc} ties the books in a cloth, puts on the one good robe, and sets off for the capital alone, over the pass at night to save a day. The pass at night has wolves, and worse. {He} knows you are out there somewhere. {He} walks faster anyway.

choices.text: Walk beside {him}, unseen, the whole way

mem.note: walked me over the pass at night

effects.log: All night, a shadow in the trees at the edge of the path. At the top of the pass {npc} stops and bows to the dark, deeply, the way one bows to an examiner. Then {he} goes down toward the capital. You watch until the dawn swallows {him}.

choices.text: Walk where {he} can see you

mem.note: walked beside me all night over the pass

effects.log: You walk beside {him} in the open, a striped shape a few paces off. {npc} is terrified for the first mile and then talks to you the rest of the way: the examination, the old books, the family at home who sold a field for this. You learn more about humans that night than in your whole life.

choices.text: Let {him} go alone. The debt is paid

effects.log: You stay on your ridge. {npc} crosses the pass alone and safe, as it happens. You tell yourself the debt is paid. It does not feel paid. Some debts are not the kind that end.

events.text: Dusk on the hill road, late autumn. A woman comes up from the valley with a basket on her head and rice cakes in it: she has pounded rice at a rich house's feast all day, and the cakes are her wages, for her children at home over the hills. At the top of the first hill your brother Torn-Ear is sitting in the road. You are in the bushes above. Torn-Ear cannot speak to her. He does not need to. He looks at the basket. She throws him a rice cake, and he lets her pass.

choices.text: Follow, and watch

effects.log: The second hill: Torn-Ear is in the road again, having gone round by the ridge. Another rice cake. The third hill, another. The basket is getting light. The woman has started to cry without slowing down.

choices.text: Get to the next hill first and sit in the road

effects.log: You sit in the road at the second hill. Torn-Ear comes round the ridge, sees you, and stops. The woman sees two tigers and stands absolutely still. Torn-Ear grins. "Share, then," he says, and goes round you to the third hill.

choices.text: Sit beside Torn-Ear and take a rice cake too

effects.log: The woman throws two. Rice cakes are sticky and sweet and taste of somebody else's feast. Torn-Ear gives you an approving look, which is the worst thing that happens to you that year.

events.text: The last hill before her village. The basket is empty. Torn-Ear is in the road, and he has stopped pretending it was about rice cakes. He looks back at you over his shoulder. "Her clothes will fit one of us," he says. "She has children at home. Children open the door for their mother."

choices.text: Stop him

ok.log: You hit him from the side and the two of you go off the road and down the slope in a ball of teeth. When you come up, the woman is gone, running, the empty basket left in the road. Torn-Ear limps off without a word. He will remember.

fail.log: He is bigger and hungrier, and he throws you down the slope. When you climb back up, the road is empty except for a basket and a scrap of white cloth. (-20 health)

choices.text: Roar her home: let the village hear

effects.log: You roar from the hilltop and the whole valley rings with it. The village below bursts into gongs and torches. The woman runs the last stretch with her skirts in her fists. Torn-Ear looks at you as if you had bitten him. You have, in a way.

choices.text: Do nothing. He is your brother

effects.log: You look away. When you look back there is only the basket in the road. Later Torn-Ear comes back up the hill with a bundle of white clothes in his mouth and puts it down at your feet.

events.text: The clothes are hers: the white jacket, the long skirt, the headcloth, still warm. Torn-Ear pushes them at you with his nose. "You are the smaller," he says. "They will fit you. The children will see the skirt at the door and open it. We share."

choices.text: Put them on

effects.log: The skirt goes on over your hind legs. The jacket will not close. The headcloth slides over one ear. In the dark it will do. You go down the hill toward a house with a light in it, walking on your hind legs, badly.

choices.text: Refuse, and run ahead to the house

effects.log: You leave him with the clothes and run down to the house first. You cannot warn them; you have no words they would understand. You can only be there.

choices.text: Tear the clothes to pieces

effects.log: You shred them across the hillside. Torn-Ear watches, and then, very calmly, goes down to the house anyway. "Children," he says over his shoulder, "also open the door for a voice."

events.text: Night. A thatched house, a paper door, a lamp inside, and two small voices: a brother and a sister. You are standing on your hind legs in their mother's skirt. In the bushes Torn-Ear makes the voice for you, high and cracked: "Open the door, children, Mother is home." "Mother's voice is not so rough," says the boy. "Show us your hand."

choices.text: Push your paw through the paper door

effects.log: Your paw comes through the paper, striped and huge. "Mother's hand is not so rough," says the girl. "It is rough from pounding rice all day," croaks Torn-Ear from the bushes. A silence. Then the boy sees the tail under the door, and there is a crash at the back of the house, and they are gone.

choices.text: Drop to all fours and walk away

effects.log: You step out of the skirt in the yard and go. Behind you Torn-Ear is still talking in a dead woman's voice. Then a crash at the back of the house: they have heard him, and they are out of the window and gone.

choices.text: Let your tail show under the door

effects.log: You turn so that your tail lies across the threshold, under the door, in the lamplight. A gasp inside. A crash at the back. Two small shapes are out of the back window and running for the big tree by the well before Torn-Ear understands what you have done.

events.text: Night. Torn-Ear stands at the paper door of the thatched house, talking in the dead woman's voice, or what he can make of it, and two children inside are not sure. "Show us your hand," says the boy. You are in the yard, in the dark, with no words at all.

choices.text: Knock over the jars on the jar platform

effects.log: Crash, and crash, and a jar of soy sauce rolling across the yard. The children scream and are out of the back window and up the big tree by the well while Torn-Ear is still turning round.

choices.text: Lie down across the threshold

ok.log: You lie across the doorstep between your brother and the door. He snarls; you do not move. Inside, the children hear two tigers and do the only sensible thing: out of the back window and up the big tree by the well.

fail.log: He drags you off the step by the scruff. But the noise is enough. The children are out of the back window and up the big tree by the well. (-15 health)

choices.text: Do nothing

effects.log: You stay in the dark. They ask for his hand, and he shows it, and the girl sees his tail under the door. The children are out of the back window and up the big tree by the well before he is through the paper.

events.text: The children are high in the old tree by the well, as high as the branches go, holding each other. Torn-Ear is at the bottom, clawing at the bark and sliding back. The girl looks up at the sky and says, very clearly, "Heaven, if you mean to save us, send down a strong rope." And a rope comes down. Out of the night, out of nothing: thick and new, smelling of rice straw and frost. The children climb it, and are gone.

choices.text: Watch them go, and be glad

effects.log: Up and up, two small shapes against the stars, until they are among the stars. The next morning the sun rises a little brighter than you remember it, and that night, the moon. You do not know yet what you saw. You are glad anyway.

choices.text: Wish for a rope of your own

effects.log: You look at the rope and want one too, more than you have ever wanted anything: a way up, out of the stripes, out of the hunger. The wanting frightens you. You put it away somewhere deep, and it waits there.

choices.text: Watch Torn-Ear

effects.log: Torn-Ear stares up at the rope with his mouth open. Then he asks the sky for one too, in the voice of the dead woman. Nothing comes, this time. He goes off into the dark, furious. You think: one day, for someone, something will.

events.text: Years later. On the flat rock at the top of the first hill, every autumn on the same day, there is a rice cake, sometimes three. The woman you saw home that night is grey now. She sets them down and says to the bushes, to nobody, "For the one who walked me home," and goes on over the hill without looking round.

choices.text: Eat them, every year

effects.log: Sticky, sweet, a little stale from the walk. You eat them every year until the year they stop coming. That year you go down the hill and find the fresh grave, and lie beside it for one night.

choices.text: Leave them for the children who come after

effects.log: You leave them. The village children find them and decide the rock is lucky. Three generations of children touch it before they cross the hill. The rice cakes keep coming.

choices.text: Let her see you, once

effects.log: She sees you in the bushes. She does not run. She bows, a small bow, a neighbour bowing to a neighbour. You lower your head. She tells her grandchildren about it, and they do not believe a word.

events.text: A dome of clay on the mountainside, smoking from a hole at the top, and beside it an old man black to the elbows with soot: a charcoal burner, tending his kiln all night, alone. One of his straw sandals is new and one is old. It is the coldest night of the winter, and the warmth coming off the clay reaches you in the trees. He sees your eyes. He does not reach for his axe. "Well, come and get warm, then," he says. "The kiln does not mind who it warms."

choices.text: Come and lie in the warmth

effects.log: You lie down at the very edge of the light with the heat of the clay on your face. The old man talks: about oak, which must be cut in winter; about the kiln, which must be sealed for four days and must not breathe; about his wife, nine years dead. You fall asleep. He keeps talking.

choices.text: Stay in the trees and listen

effects.log: He talks into the dark anyway, all night, to the trees and to you. In the morning he leaves half a barley ball on a stone, just in case.

choices.text: Show your teeth and go

effects.log: He nods, as if that were a fair answer. "Suit yourself," he says. You go, colder. You come back the next night anyway, and he is still talking.

events.text: All that winter you come to the kiln. The old man has named you Stripes, which is not very clever, and he tells you everything: which hillsides have good oak, how to tell from the smoke when the charcoal is done, how his wife laughed, how the county clerk cheats him on the weight. When the kiln is opened he draws out the charcoal in long grey-white sticks that ring like bells when they touch.

choices.text: Bring him a hare for his pot

effects.log: He looks at the hare, then at you. "Now that," he says, "is a neighbour." He makes a stew and talks to you about it all the while it cooks.

choices.text: Lie with your back to the warm clay

effects.log: The kiln is warm as a mother. You sleep against it, and he leans against you, an old man and a young tiger, and neither of you mentions it.

choices.text: Learn the smoke

effects.log: White smoke: the wood is drying. Yellow: it is burning. Blue and thin: it is done. You will read smoke on the mountains all your life and think of him.

events.text: Late, the kiln sealed and breathing, the old man asleep on his straw mat in its warmth. A shape comes out of the trees across the clearing, low, the way your mother taught all of you: Torn-Ear, grown. He is not looking at you. He is looking at the sleeper. He knows this smell. He has known it since a sandal, years ago.

choices.text: Stand over the old man

ok.log: You stand over the sleeping man and do not move, and when Torn-Ear comes you meet him across the kiln. It is short and ugly. He goes back into the trees bleeding. The old man sleeps through all of it, and in the morning finds the blood, and does not ask.

fail.log: He nearly kills you. But the noise wakes the old man, who beats on the kiln door with his iron rake until the whole mountain rings, and Torn-Ear goes. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: your own brother, beside a charcoal kiln

choices.text: Wake him: roar

effects.log: You roar at the sleeper. He comes up off the mat with the iron rake in both hands, sees two tigers, and backs against the kiln. Torn-Ear looks at you a long moment, and goes. The old man leaves the mountain that spring. You never hear him talk again.

choices.text: Step aside. He is your brother

effects.log: You step aside. You do not watch. In the morning the kiln has gone cold because nobody tended it, the charcoal is spoiled, and there is one straw sandal in the clearing. For the rest of your life the smell of charcoal smoke will turn your stomach.

events.text: In a cave above the tree line lives a she-bear so old that her muzzle is white and the crescent on her chest has gone the colour of weak tea. Everything on the mountain leaves her alone: not because she is dangerous, but because she knows things. You come to her cave mouth on a winter dusk because you smell mugwort, which bears do not eat.
events.arc: The Bear Who Knows the Story

choices.text: Ask her why she keeps mugwort

effects.log: "For remembering," she says. "Come in out of the snow, striped one. Your kind and mine have a story between us. Has nobody told you?"

choices.text: Wait to be invited

effects.log: You sit at the cave mouth until she says, "Well, come in, then. You are letting the warmth out." Manners, from a tiger. She seems to find it touching.

choices.text: Leave. Bears are trouble

effects.log: You go. She calls after you, unhurried: "Your ancestor left early too." You stop. You do not turn round. You come back the next night.

events.text: "Long ago," says the old bear, "a bear and a tiger lived in one cave, and prayed to the son of heaven to be made human. He gave them a bundle of mugwort and twenty cloves of garlic and said: eat this, and do not see the sun for a hundred days. My ancestor stayed. Yours," and she looks at you with her small bright eyes, "was hungry. On the twentieth day, or so they say, your ancestor walked out into the sun."
events.arc: The Bear Who Knows the Story

choices.text: Why would anyone want to be human?

effects.log: "I have asked myself that for a hundred winters," says the bear. "They are cold, and weak, and they die so fast. And still. Look at their fires. Listen to their songs." She hums one, badly.

choices.text: Your ancestor was right. Garlic is not food

effects.log: The bear laughs until she coughs. "That is what yours said," she says. "Almost exactly."

choices.text: What happened to the bear?

effects.log: "Wait," she says. "That is the next part. Bears tell stories slowly. That is also why we got to the hundredth day."

events.text: "On the twenty-first day," says the old bear, "my ancestor walked out of the cave on two legs, a woman. But nobody would take a bear-woman into his house, so she went to the sandalwood tree on the mountain and prayed every day for a child. The son of heaven heard, and she bore a son, and he founded the first kingdom. Every king since has had a bear in the cave of his blood. And every tiger," she says gently, "has had twenty days."
events.arc: The Bear Who Knows the Story

choices.text: I could stay longer than twenty

effects.log: "Could you?" says the bear, and looks at your belly, which is growling. "We shall see. The cave is still there, they say. It does not close."

choices.text: Tigers do not need kings

effects.log: "No," the bear agrees. "Tigers have mountains instead. It is not a worse bargain. Only a different one."

choices.text: Ask her where the cave is

effects.log: She tells you: a long way north, under the great white mountain, behind a fall of pale stones. "Not yet," she says. "You are far too young to be that hungry for anything but meat."

events.text: The old bear does not come out in spring. You find her at the back of the cave, curled round the last bundle of mugwort, breathing as slowly as snow falls. "Striped one," she says. "Take the mugwort. Not to eat. To remember that a hundred days is only a hundred days."
events.arc: The Bear Who Knows the Story

choices.text: Take it

effects.log: You carry the dry bundle out in your mouth. It is bitter. You keep it at the back of your den for years, until it is dust, and then you keep the dust.

choices.text: Stay with her to the end

effects.log: You lie at the cave mouth for nine days, keeping the wolves off. On the tenth she stops breathing, between one word of a song and the next. You stay one day more, for manners.

choices.text: Leave it with her

effects.log: You push the bundle back against her, and she understands, and smiles with her white muzzle. The cave keeps her, and the mugwort, and the story. You will come back for it one day, or you will not.

events.text: You have no mother's mountain now, and no den but the one you dig. On a ridge between two valleys, where the deer cross and the wind carries well, you stop under a great oak. Every tiger that ever held this ridge has scratched this tree. The oldest marks have healed into the bark like scars. The newest is three winters old. Nobody holds it now.

choices.text: Rear up and scratch higher than the oldest mark

ok.log: Up on your hind legs, stretched to the end of your reach, claws in, and down: four white grooves above every other tiger's. The ridge is yours, if you can hold it.

fail.log: Your marks come out below three old tigers' marks. It will do. A low mark that is held is better than a high one abandoned.

choices.text: Scent the whole bound before you claim it

effects.log: Three days walking the ridgeline: the boundary pines, the stream, a split rock. You spray and scrape at every one, so that anything that reads the mountain reads you.

choices.text: Wait a season, and see who comes

effects.log: You hunt quietly and mark nothing. Nobody comes to the oak. In autumn you scratch it, knowing exactly what you are claiming.

events.text: Wolves. Seven of them, grey and lean, and this was their ridge before it was yours: they have been reading your marks all winter and have decided to disagree. They come at dusk, spread in a fan across the snow, the old she-wolf in front.

choices.text: Hold the oak and fight

ok.log: You put your back to the oak and they come from three sides. It is long. When it is over, two wolves lie in the snow and the rest are on the far ridge, howling about it. The oak is yours.

fail.log: They take you from behind while the old one holds your eyes. You get away to the cliffs, torn all over, and lie up for a month. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: a wolf pack, on your first ridge

choices.text: Go for the old she-wolf only

ok.log: You ignore the others and go straight through them to the leader. One blow. She rolls in the snow, gets up, and limps away, and the pack goes with her. Strength in the right place beats strength in many places.

fail.log: She is old and clever and not where you strike. The pack bites at your legs until you back up against the oak. They go at dawn, unconvinced. (-15 health)

choices.text: Share: the ridge has room for wolves below the oak

effects.log: You hold the top of the ridge and let them have the gully. It takes a winter of snarling to settle. Afterwards they eat what you leave, and warn you of hunters with their howling. A strange, practical peace.

events.text: A full year on the ridge, your marks on every boundary tree, renewed every few days. One morning there is a new scent on the great oak: a young tiger from the north, passing through, who has scratched just below your marks, carefully. A polite question.

choices.text: Answer with a mark above theirs

effects.log: You scratch higher and deeper. The stranger reads it and goes on south. The question is answered. The ridge is yours.

choices.text: Find the stranger and see them off

ok.log: You find them at the stream at dusk. A great deal of noise, very little blood. They go south fast. Everything on the ridge heard it, which was the point.

fail.log: They are bigger than their marks suggested. You both bleed. In the end they shrug and go on south, because they were passing through anyway. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let them pass. Mark nothing

effects.log: They pass through and do not come back. A young tiger does not have to answer every question. But your neighbours, the wolves and the boars, noticed that you did not.

events.text: Somebody has rubbed out your mark on the boundary pine: a big black bear, scratching its back against it, leaving its own musty smell all over yours, and a tuft of black hair in the resin.

choices.text: Mark it again, higher

effects.log: You scratch the pine above where any bear can reach. The bear reads it the next day, sits down, and thinks about it. Bears think slowly. It goes away in the end.

choices.text: Have a word with the bear

ok.log: You find it in the berry thicket. A short conversation, mostly teeth. It decides there are other pines in the world.

fail.log: It stands up. It is a great deal taller standing up. You decide there are other pines in the world. (-14 health)

choices.text: Let the bear have the pine. There are others

effects.log: You move the bound back one pine. It costs nothing but pride. The bear never knows it won.

events.text: Rain from a clear sky. The sun is out, the sky is blue from edge to edge, and big warm drops are falling on the rocks, each one lit up like a bead. Your mother lifts her head and watches it, and so does every animal on the mountain. "A tiger is taking a mate somewhere," she says. "That is what this rain is. A tiger's wedding."

choices.text: Ask whose wedding

effects.log: "Nobody knows," she says. "Somebody far off. The sky cries a little and laughs a little at the same time. That is a wedding."

choices.text: Run out into it

effects.log: You run round the rocks with your mouth open, catching rain in the sunshine. Your brothers join you. For one afternoon nobody bites anybody.

choices.text: Look at the far ridge

effects.log: Through the shining rain, on the far ridge, you think you see something moving: a line of shapes walking one behind another, slow and stately. Then the mist comes, and it is gone.

events.text: Another sunshower, years later, and this time you are watching for it. On the far ridge, through the bright rain and the mist rising off the warm stones, a procession of tigers walks one behind another along the skyline: old ones in front, slow; then two walking shoulder to shoulder; then young ones, and cubs, tumbling. No sound reaches you at all.

choices.text: Keep pace along your own ridge

ok.log: You keep pace with them along the opposite ridge until the rain stops. As the last drop falls they turn their heads, all of them, and look at you across the valley. Then the sun is only sun, and the ridge is empty.

fail.log: You slip on the wet rock, and when you look up the rain has stopped and the ridge is bare.

choices.text: Lie still and watch

effects.log: You watch until the rain stops. You do not know whose wedding it was. You know you would like one, one day, on a ridge in the rain. It is the first time you have wanted something that is not food.

choices.text: Roar a greeting

effects.log: You roar across the valley. On the far ridge one tiger at the very back of the procession stops and looks at you for a long moment before it goes on.

events.text: The first sunshower of the year, and when it stops you find fresh tracks on your own boundary: a tiger of the next mountain, about your age, who has walked the length of your ridge, stopped at your oak, and done nothing at all. Only looked. On the stone below the oak, very neatly, they have left a dead pheasant.

choices.text: Leave something in return at their boundary

effects.log: You take a hare to the stream that divides the two mountains and leave it on the far bank. Next sunshower there is a pheasant on your stone again. It goes on like that: a slow courtesy across a stream.

choices.text: Follow the tracks home

ok.log: You find them at dusk, lying on a rock on the next mountain, watching the sun go down. They see you. Neither of you moves. You go home before dark, and think about it for a year.

fail.log: The tracks go into a stream and do not come out. Clever. You find you like them more for it.

choices.text: Eat the pheasant and mark your oak twice

effects.log: Delicious, and very clearly yours. The tracks do not come back. Perhaps that was the answer you meant to give. Afterwards you are not sure.

events.text: In the oak wood on the far side of your ridge you find the bones of a tiger, a big one, its ribs split. A season later, a second tiger, by the stream. Both times the ground around is torn up as if by a plough. The wolves will not go into that wood. The magpie will not even talk about it. The boars of the mountain call it Iron-Tusk, and they say it with pride.

choices.text: Go and look for the boar

effects.log: You find its wallow: a hollow of black mud as big as a threshing floor, and on the oak beside it a tusk mark higher than your head. You come home very thoughtful.

choices.text: Learn about it from the bones

effects.log: Both tigers were taken from the side, low, the tusk going up under the ribs. Both were taken in the leap. You decide that if you ever meet it, you will not leap.

choices.text: Stay out of the oak wood

effects.log: There are other woods. You keep to them. But the acorns are in the oak wood, and the deer go where the acorns are, and you are hungry that winter.

events.text: It finds you, in the end. A hot afternoon in the oak mast, and a noise behind you like a loaded cart coming down a hill, and there it is: black, its bristles grey as iron, as big as an ox, with tusks as long as your forelegs. It has killed two tigers. It looks at you as if you would make three.

choices.text: Climb the cliff where it cannot follow

effects.log: Up the rocks, fast. It hits the cliff behind you so hard that stones fall. It waits at the bottom until dark, and then it goes. You come down at dawn, alive, and ashamed of nothing.

choices.text: Fight it on the slope

ok.log: You do not leap. You let it come, you turn, you take it from the side, low, the way it took them, and you hold on while it drags you through the whole oak wood. When it stops, it does not get up. The boars of the mountain talk about it for years, without pride.

fail.log: The tusk goes up under your ribs, exactly as the bones said it would. You get away into the rocks with your side opened and lie there a month, not knowing which day will be the last. (-35 health)
fail.deathCause: Iron-Tusk, the boar that killed tigers

choices.text: Lead it over the old pit on the game trail

ok.log: You run, it follows, you jump the patch of leaves you know too well, and it does not. The crash shakes the gully. In the morning the village hunters find the biggest boar anyone has ever seen at the bottom of their pit, and are very proud of themselves.

fail.log: It does not follow you over the leaves; it goes round. Iron-Tusk has not lived this long by falling into pits. It catches you at the end of the gully. (-20 health)

events.text: Iron-Tusk again, years older, slower, one tusk broken off short and angrier for it. It has come into your territory to root under your marked oak, as if to tell you something about whose mountain this is.

choices.text: Fight it now. It is old

ok.log: Old, and still the strongest thing you have ever fought. But one tusk is not two. When the dust settles under the oak it is lying in the hole it dug, and you are standing.

fail.log: The broken tusk is still a tusk. It opens your shoulder and goes off through the oak wood at a trot, as if it had only been passing. (-30 health)

choices.text: Let it root. It is old

effects.log: You watch it from the rocks. It digs under your oak for a day and goes away. A year later you find it dead of age in its wallow, and nothing on the mountain has touched it. You do not either.

choices.text: Drive it off with a roar

ok.log: You roar from the ridge with everything you have. The old boar lifts its head, considers you, and goes. Not afraid. Tired. You understand that better than you would like.

fail.log: It does not care about your roar. It cares about your oak. You give the oak up for a season. (-12 health)

events.text: With Iron-Tusk gone, the oak wood fills up again: deer, badgers, the wolves, and boars, ordinary ones, with ordinary tusks. They give your ridge a wide berth now. The magpie has finally found its voice about the whole business and tells it to everyone, with improvements.

choices.text: Eat well this winter

effects.log: Acorn-fat deer and boars all winter. You come out of it heavier in the shoulder than you have ever been.

choices.text: Lie on the wallow and let the mountain see

effects.log: You lie in the middle of Iron-Tusk's wallow in full sun. Every creature that passes looks. You enjoy it rather more than a tiger should.

choices.text: Leave the oak wood to the deer for a season

effects.log: The oak wood has been a killing ground for years. You let it be a wood for a while. The deer grow fat and careless, and so, next autumn, do you.

events.text: A winter with no deer. They went south ahead of the snow, all of them, and the boars have dug in somewhere you cannot find. You have eaten a badger, a frozen crow, the scraps of a hare. Your ribs show through your stripes. Down in the valley the village dogs are barking, fat and warm and stupid.

choices.text: Take a dog from the edge of the village

effects.log: A yellow dog on a straw rope by a gate. It barks once. In the morning the village finds the rope and the tracks, and the old people say the mountain lord has come down hungry, and set a bowl of millet by the shrine, which you do not eat.

choices.text: Hold out on the mountain

effects.log: You chew frozen bark and snow and wait. Hunger is a teacher. It teaches only one thing, over and over. (-12 health)

choices.text: Go further north for deer

ok.log: Four days north, in a valley nobody has hunted all winter, you find them yarded in the snow. You eat, and sleep, and eat.

fail.log: Four days north and nothing, and four days back. (-10 health)

events.text: Deeper into winter. You are standing in the snow behind a farmhouse, and through the slats of the cowshed you can smell a calf: milk-sweet, warm, half asleep against its mother. The family is asleep beyond a paper door. They are poor; you can tell from the roof. One calf is their whole spring.

choices.text: Take the calf

effects.log: The shed door gives. The cow bellows. You are on the mountain with the calf before the lamp is lit. That spring the family ploughs by hand, father and son in the traces. You know, because you watch them.

choices.text: Take nothing. Walk away

effects.log: You stand in the snow until your paws ache, and then you go back up the mountain with nothing. It is the hardest thing you have done. Nobody will ever know you did it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Take a hen from the headman's yard instead

effects.log: A hen from the headman's yard, who has forty. It is almost nothing to eat. It is almost nothing to lose. You feel that is a kind of justice, and you are a little proud of it, and still hungry.

events.text: Dusk, the village path at the foot of your mountain. An old woman comes up it alone with a bundle of pine needles for kindling on her back, bent nearly double. She is last; the others went home an hour ago. She is small. She is warm. You can hear her heart from the bushes. The hunger says one word, over and over, and it is not a word you like.

choices.text: Turn and go up the mountain

effects.log: You turn. Every step up the mountain is heavy. Behind you she sings to herself on the path, some old song about a magpie, not knowing. You will remember that song when you are very old.

choices.text: Walk behind her, guarding her, to her gate

effects.log: You follow her all the way to the village, a shadow keeping the wolves off, with the hunger walking beside you like a third. At her gate she turns and sees you, and does not scream. "Ah," she says. "So it was you." She shuts the gate. You go home hungrier, and lighter.

choices.text: Show yourself, and let fear do it instead

effects.log: You step onto the path. She drops the pine needles and runs, faster than you would have thought, and the whole village comes out with gongs. Nobody is hurt; you made sure. But you liked her running, and you will have to think about that.

choices.text: Take one step after her

effects.log: One step. Then another. Then a dog barks at the village gate and a gong starts, and you wake out of it standing in the middle of the path with your mouth open. You run up the mountain as if something were chasing you. Something was.

events.text: Hungry again. It never goes far. It lies in your belly like a second tiger, and this winter it is the bigger of the two. From the ridge you can see three villages and smell every hearth in them.

choices.text: Hunt hard, whatever it costs

ok.log: Three days on the track of a red deer stag through the snow, and on the third evening he stumbles at the frozen stream. The hunger lies down, for now.

fail.log: You run down a lame hind after a week. It is skin and bone. So are you. (-12 health)

choices.text: Raid a village pigsty

effects.log: A fat pig through a broken fence, and the whole village awake and banging pots behind you. That is one less hungry tiger and one more angry village.

choices.text: Eat what the wolves leave

effects.log: Scraps from the wolves' kill in the gully. They watch you eat their leavings with deep contempt. It is enough. Pride does not fill a belly.

events.text: Men on the game trail at the bottom of the gully, six of them, with mattocks and baskets and a pile of sharpened stakes, their points hardened black in a fire. They dig all morning, talking about the cow a tiger took last winter from the next valley. Not you. A tiger. To them it is the same thing.

choices.text: Watch exactly how they do it

effects.log: You watch them dig, set the stakes, lay thin poles across, and leaves over the poles. You learn the look of it, and the smell of fresh earth under old leaves. You will never forget either.

choices.text: Drive them off before they finish

effects.log: You roar from the ferns. They drop the mattocks and run. They come back the next week with twice as many men and finish the pit anyway, and now they know a tiger was watching.

choices.text: Leave. It is not your trail

effects.log: You go round to the other side of the mountain. That winter a deer goes into the pit, and the men are pleased, and so are you, a little: better a deer.

events.text: A boy from the village, ten or eleven years old, has decided to be a tiger hunter.
