He comes up the mountain alone with a short spade and a bundle of sharpened sticks and digs his own pit, right across your path to the stream: a hole up to his waist, the sticks pointing up, a handful of leaves on top. It would not catch a badger. He is enormously proud of it.

choices.text: Step over it, so he finds your tracks on both sides

effects.log: In the morning the boy finds the tracks: up to the pit, over it, on. He stands there a long time. Then he fills it in, and when he grows up he does not become a tiger hunter.

choices.text: Step in it on purpose, and climb out

effects.log: You step in it, sticks and all, and climb out and go on. In the morning he finds the broken sticks and runs all the way down to the village shouting that he nearly caught the tiger. Nobody believes him. He is happy for a year. (-5 health)

choices.text: Show yourself to him, once

effects.log: He looks up from his digging and you are on the bank above him. He does not run. He holds up his spade. You look at each other for a long time. Then you go. You think that one will come back, with a better spade.

events.text: You are careful on the game trail now, but the men have learned too. This time there is no pit. There is a man in a blind of cut brushwood beside the path, very still, with a spear, and you smell him exactly one breath too late.

choices.text: Spring past him

ok.log: The spear comes out of the brushwood and grazes your flank. You are past and gone. A shallow cut and a long lesson. (-6 health)

fail.log: The spear goes into your shoulder. You tear free and run with the shaft hanging from you, and pull it out with your teeth on the ridge. You have a scar now where your mother had hers. (-20 health)

choices.text: Turn on him

ok.log: You go through the brushwood and the man and the spear in one rush, and leave him in the path with his arm broken and his face in the leaves. You do not bite. You are not sure why not. (-10 health)

fail.log: He is braver than you expected and the spear is longer. It goes into your shoulder as you come. You break off and run. (-22 health)

choices.text: Freeze in the ferns

ok.log: You stop where you are, one paw lifted. He does not see you. You back away a step at a time all the way to the ridge, and he sits in his blind until dark, waiting for a tiger that has already gone home.

fail.log: He sees the ferns move. The spear takes you in the haunch. (-15 health)

events.text: The road over the pass below your ridge is a woodcutters' road. They go up in the morning with empty A-frames and come down in the evening with firewood stacked above their heads, and they never, ever come alone: they wait at the bottom for each other and cross together, a long line with a gong. You lie on the rocks above and watch them every evening.

choices.text: Count them

effects.log: One, and one, and one. You did not know you could count. It turns out you can: ten, most evenings. On market days, twelve. Once, nine, and the whole line kept looking back, again and again, the way your mother used to look back for you.

choices.text: Watch the last one in the line

effects.log: The last one in line is always the nervous one. They take it in turns, you notice. Somebody has told them that a tiger takes the last in line. Somebody is right, about some tigers.

choices.text: Learn the gong

effects.log: Clang, a step, clang. The gong is to tell you they are coming. It is, you realise, a kind of courtesy. You get out of the road.

events.text: The line goes over the pass at dusk, and at the back of it, falling further behind with every step, is an old woodcutter with a bad leg and a load too big for him. The gong is far ahead now. He stops to rest on a rock right under yours, wipes his face, and knows exactly where he is.

choices.text: Walk down the slope behind him, at a distance, all the way

effects.log: You keep pace with him in the trees all the way down. Near the bottom he turns, sees your eyes, and says quite calmly, "Thank you, mountain lord," and goes on. You did not know you had a title.

choices.text: Knock a stone down to hurry him

effects.log: The stone clatters past him. He is up and gone on his bad leg faster than any of the young ones. Fear is a strong medicine. It is also a bitter one.

choices.text: Watch him. Only watch

effects.log: He sits, and rests, and goes, and nothing happens. But you watched him the way your brothers watch, and you both knew it. He crosses in the middle of the line after that.

events.text: A night crossing, which nobody makes: porters with a load the magistrate wants by morning, eleven of them, with torches and the gong going all the time, and a drum, and someone singing loudly to show he is not afraid. They are all very afraid. You are lying beside the road in the dark, close enough to touch the last one.

choices.text: Let them pass, and count every one

effects.log: Eleven torches in, eleven torches out on the far side of the pass. You count them twice to be sure. You like it when the count comes out the same at both ends.

choices.text: Put out the last torch with one breath

effects.log: One breath, and the last torch goes out. Eleven men run the rest of the pass in the dark, shrieking the whole way, and by the next day the whole county knows the pass belongs to a tiger. The magistrate gets his load at noon instead of dawn.

choices.text: Walk ahead of them in the dark, keeping the wolves off

effects.log: Somewhere ahead of the torches the wolves of the pass smell you and decide on a different evening. The porters cross without trouble and never know why. In the morning they say the gong worked.

events.text: The snow begins in the tenth month and does not stop. It comes up to your shoulders, then to your back. The deer are yarded somewhere you cannot reach, and every step you take is a leap. The whole mountain is white and silent, and you are a striped thing in it that everything can see.

choices.text: Keep to the ridges where the wind clears the snow

effects.log: The wind has swept the ridgelines down to stone. You walk along them like a rope-dancer and look down on a world buried to the eaves.

choices.text: Dig in and wait it out

effects.log: A den under a fallen pine, snow over the roof like a lid. You sleep, wake hungry, sleep. (-8 health)

choices.text: Follow the wild boars' trench

effects.log: The boars have ploughed a trench through the snow to the acorns, and where boars go, sooner or later, a tiger can eat.

events.text: Weeks of snow. You find a dead red deer at the bottom of a ravine, fallen and frozen, and on it, already eating, a single grey wolf, alone, as thin as you are. It does not run. It cannot. It lifts its lip at you and goes on eating, because it would rather die fed.

choices.text: Share it

effects.log: You go to the other end of the carcass and eat. The wolf watches you, and eats, and watches you. Neither of you goes for the other. In the morning you are both still alive, which is more than either of you expected.

choices.text: Drive it off

effects.log: It goes, slowly, looking back. You eat it all. The wolf's tracks go up the ravine and stop in a drift two days later. You do not go to look.

choices.text: Let it have the deer

effects.log: You turn and go. You do not know why. Something about the way it would rather die fed. You are hungry for another week. (-8 health)

events.text: Spring at last: the snow gone grey and rotten, water running under it everywhere. On the ridge one morning stands the lone wolf from the ravine, and behind it a pack: five, six, young and thin. It looks at you, and then turns and leads them away north. At the end of the ravine, on a flat stone, there is a fresh-killed hare.

choices.text: Eat the hare

effects.log: A hare is a small thing. From a starving wolf it is not. You eat it slowly.

choices.text: Follow them to the edge of your bounds

effects.log: They go north, out of your mountains. A debt between a wolf and a tiger is a strange thing, and settled now. You will hear wolves on the far ridge on cold nights for the rest of your life, and wonder.

choices.text: Leave the hare on the stone

effects.log: You leave it. It was not payment. It was a word, and you have heard it. The magpie eats the hare.

events.text: Your fur has been changing all summer. The cub fluff has come out in tufts on every bush, and under it the stripes have come in black and hard, black on gold, as if someone had painted you with ink while you slept. Your brothers look like tigers. So, presumably, do you.

choices.text: Look in the stream

effects.log: In the still pool below the falls, a tiger looks back at you. You do not recognise it. It does not recognise you. You stare at each other until a leaf falls on the water and breaks you both.

choices.text: Roll in the dust to see if they come off

effects.log: They do not come off. You check again the next day.

choices.text: Count them

effects.log: You lose count at forty and start again, and lose count at forty again. Somewhere on your left flank there are seven stripes in a row that look almost like something: a shape you have seen in the western sky at night. You do not know what yet.

events.text: In the same pool, years later, the tiger looking back is not a cub at all: long, heavy in the shoulder, with a face that wolves step off the path for. The stripes are as dark as they will ever be. And at the very tip of your tail, if you look closely, a few hairs have come in pale.

choices.text: Admire it

effects.log: You admire it for some time. A magpie on a branch over the pool admires you admiring it, and laughs.

choices.text: Look at the pale hairs

effects.log: Three or four hairs, white as the first frost. Old tigers go grey, you suppose. You are not old. You look at them a long time anyway, as if they were a message. They are.

choices.text: Go and hunt. Stripes are for hunting

effects.log: You leave the pool and take a roe deer before dark, and do not think about your reflection again for years.
